explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing ‘the same thing’ – they return for each t2 row (a beer) either (a) no t5 row (if none exists) or (b) only those t5 rows whose price equals the minimum price computed over t5 for that beer. In Q1 the minimum price is pre‐computed in a derived table (the GROUP BY subquery) and then used in the ON clause of a second LEFT JOIN. In Q2 the minimum price is recomputed (via a scalar correlated subquery) inside the WHERE clause (using the condition “alias2.c3 IS NULL OR alias2.c3 = ( … MIN … )”). Although in many cases the two queries return the same “beer – price – supplier” rows, they are not semantically equivalent. In particular the placement of the “min = …” condition makes a crucial difference: the join condition in Q1 is “attached” to the outer join so that even when there are extra t5 rows for a given beer (for example, if the minimum price appears more than once) all minimal rows are retained. In Q2 the condition in the WHERE clause is applied after the join (and thus after the duplication from the join); in some SQL engines the filtering logic may cause different row‐multiplicity (or even loss of a row) when a t2 row has at least one t5 match that does not meet the “minimal” criterion. One may therefore “distinguish” the semantics by crafting data where a beer has duplicate minimal prices and also a “spurious” nonminimal price. (For instance, if a given beer has three rows in t5 – two with the same (minimal) price and one with a higher price – then Q1 will return two rows (one per minimal entry) while Q2’s filtering (applied row‐by‐row after the join) may end up returning a different number of rows depending on how duplicate minimal rows are handled.)
counterexample_dsp: We create one t2 row (representing a beer) and three t5 rows for that beer: two of the t5 rows have the same (minimum) price and one has a higher price. Q1 (because it first aggregates t5 by beer and then joins on the minimal price) will join only with the two minimal t5 rows, whereas Q2 – because it first joins t2 to all t5 rows and then filters using the WHERE condition – may return a different number of rows (for example, if the query plan forces elimination of duplicates or if the engine ‘short‐circuits’ the OR condition, the duplicate minimal rows may not appear in the final result). This difference in row‐multiplicity distinguishes the two queries even though their basic intent is the same.
